item.title: Police and students clash in France as high school unrest intensifies
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The interior ministry said 86,000 had joined the protests, unions gave a higher figure (ROMEO BOETZLE) Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations. Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures. Unions, rights groups and the children have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force -- a police stun grenade tore the hand off one teenager on Monday and another youngster had his teeth knocked out last week after police fired a grenade launcher at his head. At the Place de la Republique in central Paris, the savoury smell of grilled merguez sausages -- a French protest staple -- wafted over the crowd. Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth". "Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen. The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction. "I'm afraid for my future," Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country's second largest city of Marseille. The interior ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier Tuesday. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people. - 'At war' - Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was "no room for tolerance of violence". "Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters. While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police. Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds. The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement. A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday. The prosecutor's office in the northeastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained. The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement. Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods. - Thousands of arrests - Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap. "We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP. Adults turned out in droves Tuesday to support the young demonstrators. Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had "talked about the police brutality we've witnessed" and decided to show up for the pupils. In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters. "As adults, we're a bit like the security cordon," she said. Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students "convey their message peacefully". "The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said. Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests". The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday. Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry. More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested. The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured. burs/giv/ah/gv This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/tens-thousands-expected-paris-high-020417724.html

item.title: Trump says taxpayers won't fund his promotional ads going forward
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them. While he dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he said he had decided to run them on his own dime rather than that of the U.S. government in a post on his social media platform. "I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC. Eric Lee/Reuters - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks with media before boarding Marine One as he travels to Grand Island, Nebraska, on the South Lawn of the White House, Oct. 5, 2026. The move comes after the U.S. government bankrolled a series of ads that aired nationally and heavily featured the president. One of the ads was a direct copy of a spot Trump's campaign ran in 2024. A White House official confirmed to ABC News Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for ads moving forward but defended them as something previous administrations have used. "Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said. Trump defends spending millions on taxpayer-funded promotional ads: 'For the country' Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance defended using taxpayer money to run the ads, claiming they are "public service announcements." "They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said. Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies. "You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said. "Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said. U.S. Government - PHOTO: A fourth taxpayer-funded ad that promotes President Donald Trump’s policies ahead of the midterm elections shows scenes of Trump and the U.S. military amid the war in Iran as audio of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the president play over them. Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates. The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television. A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort. Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law. Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country." U.S. government video - PHOTO: The Trump administration appeared to run an ad on Fox News that has drawn criticism from Democrats as violating federal rules preventing the use of tax dollars for political purposes. Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history." The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed. The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia. item.title: Who is Michele Tafoya? Ex-sideline reporter aims to turn Minnesota red in Senate race.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion’s share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers. Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red. In pursuit of that goal, the GOP has put its hopes in Michele Tafoya , a former sports broadcaster and NFL sideline reporter turned politician who polls suggest has a real chance of winning in a state that has been dominated by Democrats in recent election cycles. Tafoya is running for the seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not pursuing re-election. Instead her opponent will be Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan , a progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Minnesota has been at the center of some of the biggest controversies of President Trump’s second term, particularly his administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown. Though a majority of Minnesotans disapprove of Trump’s performance as president, Tafoya has steadily chipped away at Flanagan's lead in polls since the primary. Here’s what you need to know about who she is, what she stands for and how she went from the sidelines to the center of one of the midterms’ most pivotal races. Who is Michele Tafoya? Tafoya was born and raised in Southern California. Her father was an aeronautical engineer, and her mother was a school teacher. She has Hispanic heritage on her father’s side. She married her husband, Mark Vandersall, in 2000. They have two children. Tafoya has been open about her struggles with infertility , which included several miscarriages. Her daughter, Oliva, was adopted from Colombia as a nod to her father’s lineage. After launching her sports broadcasting career in Los Angeles, she moved to Minnesota in the early 1990s to take a job at the KFAN sports radio station in Minneapolis. Before long, she moved on to a national role with CBS, which proved to be the jumping-off point for a decades-long career that made her one of the country’s most recognizable sports broadcasters. She covered five Super Bowls, the NBA and the Olympics — winning five Emmys for her work along the way. Michele Tafoya looks on during Super Bowl LVI, the final game of her storied broadcasting career. Kevin C. Cox via Getty Images Tafoya’s last broadcast was during Super Bowl LVI in 2022. Her political career began the very next day. Less than 12 hours after the game ended, she announced that she would co-chair the campaign of Republican Kendall Qualls in his bid to become Minnesota governor. How did she go from NFL sidelines to the campaign trail? Tafoya has said she always had strong political views, but made a specific effort to keep them out of her work as a broadcaster. “I was not as free to be as vocal about world events that I’m concerned about,” she told The Athletic in 2022. “It’s not because I was told to shut up. I want to be very clear about that. But look, if you’re on a show like Sunday Night Football … the last thing they want to do is invite controversy.” Tafoya was more open about her beliefs outside on social media, where she would regularly promote work from conservative outlets . But she also made statements that broke from the GOP mainstream, including support for efforts to curb climate change. In an interview with Sports Illustrated in 2015, she described herself as a “pro-choice” conservative with “definite libertarian strains.” After retiring from broadcasting, Tafoya made several appearances as a speaker at Republican political events, including the Conservative Political Action Conference. She was also a guest host on The View , taking on the role of the conservative-leaning voice in contrast to the show’s more liberal regular panelists. In 2022, Tafoya launched a podcast that frequently touched on political topics and featured Republican politicians as guests. The most recent episode , released in January, includes an interview with former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell, who unsuccessfully ran for Minnesota governor this year despite an endorsement from President Trump. Tafoya formally announced her Senate bid a few weeks later. In August, she comfortably won a crowded Republican primary to set up a head-to-head race against Flanagan in November. What does she stand for? In her pitch to Minnesota voters, Tafoya has leaned into her sports background. “I’m not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer,” she said while standing on a snow-covered football field in her campaign announcement video. For years, I walked the sidelines when the stakes were the highest, and that job taught me how leadership really works. I’m running for U.S. Senate to bring that experience to Washington and deliver the real results Minnesota deserves. https://t.co/vDbHWpAXg9 — Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) January 21, 2026 Like other swing-state Republicans across the country, Tafoya has worked to find a balance between supporting Trump and pushing back on some of his most unpopular policies. She has supported the president throughout the war with Iran, at one point telling Minnesotans to “take one less trip to Starbucks” to help offset the rising cost of gas. More recently, though, she has joined a growing list of GOP candidates who have called for Trump to end the conflict. “No president of either party should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people. That includes President Donald Trump,” Tafoya told Twin Cities local news KSTP on Saturday. Tafoya added that she would be “inclined to vote to end this war” if given the opportunity in the Senate. She has also said she didn’t agree with ICE’s tactics in Minneapolis and described Trump’s tariff policies as “hit or miss." Her policy views mostly align with mainstream Republican positions. She backs strong immigration enforcement and Trump’s mass deportation campaign, a “tough on crime” approach to public safety, tax cuts, and laws barring transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports. On abortion, she says she agrees with the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade , but personally believes there should be “reasonable access” in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Tafoya’s own opinions of Trump have evolved as well. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Trump not to run for a second term, describing his previous time in the White House as "absolute mayhem.” She also said on her podcast around the same time that there was much about Trump that she found “difficult to accept.” But during the 2024 presidential campaign, Tafoya said she was supporting Trump with “more enthusiasm” than before. She also said she felt “sort of agnostic” on the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. She celebrated Trump’s victory later that year, describing it as “morning in America” — a reference to Ronald Reagan’s famous phrase from the 1980s. Tafoya has mostly left Trump out of her current campaign ads and speeches, instead focusing her messaging on issues like fraud, affordability and public safety. The president opted not to endorse a candidate in Minnesota’s Republican primary and has yet to throw his support behind Tafoya in the general election. What are her chances? Tafoya is one of the few Republicans in major races across the country who is outperforming expectations in the polls. In August, Flanagan held an average lead of about seven points, but Tafoya has been closing the gap . More recent surveys suggest the race is essentially up for grabs. Still, a win by Tafoya would likely be considered a significant upset. Two of the most respected non-partisan elections forecasters — The Cook Political Report and The Center for Politics — list Minnesota’s Senate race as a “likely” win for Democrats. item.title: Paramount-Warner Bros. finally merger closes, creating media giant Skydance
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The $110 billion merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed on Tuesday after Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan denied a last-minute effort to halt the deal . The new company — known as Skydance — brings the HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services under one umbrella, roughly seven months after Paramount won a long bidding war with Netflix ( NFLX ) for Warner Bros. Skydance stock began trading on Tuesday under the symbol SKYD . The merger faced plenty of pushback and a long road to closing. "The completed transaction unites two of media and entertainment's most storied companies, each with a history spanning more than a century, giving the combined business a rare legacy to build on," Skydance stated in a press release. "The aim of the combined company is to build the next-generation global media and entertainment company powered by creativity and technology." The company's entertainment franchises span "Sopranos" to "SpongeBob SquarePants" and "Euphoria" to "Harry Potter." The portfolio also encompasses television networks CBS, CBS News, CBS Sports, CNN, TNT, TBS, Nickelodeon, and MTV, among others. Last February, Warner Bros.' board of directors deemed Paramount's Skydance's $ 31-per-share proposal for the entire company "superior" to Netflix's offer . The new name is a callback to the production company that David Ellison, son of Oracle ( ORCL ) co-founder Larry Ellison , founded in 2006 and merged with Paramount in 2025. (screenshot/@davidellison/X) David Ellison will serve as co-CEO of Skydance, alongside former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz , who abruptly stepped down from the toymaker last week. On Monday, the company said Ellison will focus on long-term strategy, creative vision, and direction, "including its talent relationships, strategic partnerships, technology and capital allocation." Kreiz will focus on day-to-day management and the integration of both companies. Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News, and Mark Thompson, CNN chair and editor in chief, remain in their roles. Both were named to the CEO's News Executive Leadership Team . Paramount CFO Dennis Cinelli will hold the same role at Skydance, while other leaders are taking on new roles with higher ranks. CBS Sports chief David Berson will take over the combined sports operations as Warner Bros. Discovery's top sports executive, Luis Silberwasser, exits . HBO head Casey Bloys ‌will become Skydance's chief content officer. Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav will enjoy a nice payday to the tune of roughly $886.8 million . Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison speaks during the Paramount Pictures presentation at CinemaCon, the official convention of Cinema United, in Las Vegas on April 16, 2026. (Reuters/Caroline Brehman) Reuters / REUTERS Weeks ago, Paramount reached a settlement with a dozen states, including California , which had sought to block the company's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. on antitrust grounds. Under the agreement, the combined company would face financial penalties if it fails to release at least 30 films in theaters each year. According to two people familiar with the discussions cited by Bloomber g, Paramount would pay $30 million for each movie short of that target. The report also said Paramount could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax if it does not meet the target. In a long-shot effort to block the merger filed on Monday, four petitioners who described themselves as Paramount customers argued the merger remained anticompetitive despite the settlement. However, Supreme Court Justice Kagan denied the petition without comment. Skydance's competitors include Disney ( DIS ), Netflix, Comcast ( CMCSA ), Versant ( VSNT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Alphabet's YouTube ( GOOG , GOOGL ). "PSKY/WBD creates a new formidable global streaming competitor by putting HBO/HBO Max, Warner Bros., Paramount+, CBS, Discovery and a high quality large film & TV library under a single owner, which gives it larger bundles, broader programming options, and more asset breadth to compete for talen, sub revs and advertisers against NFLX and DIS," Needham entertainment and internet analyst Laura Martin wrote in a note Tuesday morning. item.title: Civilian cargo ship sinks and crew is missing after Black Sea drone attack
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment [Petko Momchilov / Reuters] A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say. A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable". Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said. The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania. It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board. A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain. Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan. Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law". He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable." He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning. "Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning." "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable." Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea. A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media. On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. item.title: Former Army major who killed 13 in Fort Hood shooting to be executed by firing squad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday. "Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X . He added, "The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II. The announcement of Trump's approval came days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. The failed execution prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order a third-party review. Asked whether the failed execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it "an interesting situation." He told reporters in Denton, Texas, that carrying out lethal injections "shouldn't be very difficult." Trump's approval sets in motion a series of procedural steps toward carrying out Hasan's execution. But Hasan could put the process on hold — potentially for years — by filing a habeas corpus appeal challenging the legality of his detention in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer. Hasan was convicted in a 2013 court-martial of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and was sentenced to death. He exhausted his regular appeals in 2025. What happened in the Fort Hood shooting? Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups before deploying, and witnesses testified he shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — before he opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He killed 13 people and wounded more than 30. According to the Associated Press , Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial and mounted little defense, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides." Why a firing squad rather than lethal injection? The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change. The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June. Known as Operation Resolute Justice, the plan calls for condemned service members to be transferred there from the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and for the Army to coordinate with the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Army is to be ready to carry out an execution no sooner than 60 days and within 150 days of presidential approval. ABC's report did not specify an execution method. The Justice Department separately directed the Bureau of Prisons in April to expand its protocol for federal civilian executions to include methods beyond lethal injection, including firing squads. That change does not apply to military executions. Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods. After Pike's failed execution, several top Republicans in Tennessee said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP , "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully." Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session. "We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point." How common are military executions? Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth. The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl. item.title: Trump’s daylight saving push runs into a geographic divide in the Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The battle over Americans’ clocks reemerged in an unlikely way over the weekend, with President Donald Trump picking a fight with one of his top allies over the issue. There have been many fights in Congress over the nearly two years that Trump has been in office for his second term that either ended in partisan victory or gloriously fizzled out, but one has quietly gone onto the shelf despite his pressure on Republicans to do something about it. And that fight is over allowing states to voluntarily observe daylight saving time year-round to effectively do away with the twice-a-year ritual of changing clocks. It’s a popular issue with voters and the president, and there’s a bill that passed the House this summer to enact the change. But it’s a policy issue that has divided both sides of the aisle and ground to a halt in the upper chamber. Trump Urges Senate To Pass Bill Making Daylight Saving Time Permanent After Overwhelming House Vote President Donald Trump wants to make daylight saving permanent, but a geographic coalition of northern versus southern states are in a heated debate over the merits of the change, which spells doom for the bill. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., has been one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, vowing to block any attempts to fast-track it on the floor. That resistance earned him a Truth Social post from Trump, who over the weekend shared his personal phone number in a bid to pressure the lawmaker to change his stance on daylight saving time. "Almost everybody wants "The Sunshine Protection Act" to pass, except for Tom Cotton," Trump said. "To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself." Read On The Fox News App Cotton responded, noting that Congress has tackled daylight saving time before, only to roll back the change shortly after. "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first." Trump Faces Republican Rebellion Over Daylight Saving Time As Senate Bill Nears Dead End In the 1970s, lawmakers did enact year-round daylight saving time. But Americans rapidly soured on the change, especially parents whose children had to wait in the dark for the school bus. It was repealed about a year later. And Cotton recently answered an off-the-cuff question from a fellow Republican during their weekly closed-door policy lunches, a source told Fox News Digital, where he made a similar case as his response to Trump. No one pushed back during the meeting. The issue of daylight saving time , and supporting a permanent fix or sticking to the status quo are more geographical than political. It’s, in part, mountainous and Western states versus coastal states. On one side of the spectrum are lawmakers like Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Patty Murray, D-Wash., who introduced a Senate version of the bill last year. "Every year, more Americans grow more frustrated setting their clocks back and forth, and every winter folks in Washington state despair at the prospect of losing an hour of precious sunlight when we are forced off Daylight Saving Time," Murray said in a statement at the time. House Passes Daylight Saving Time Reform As Trump Signals Support For Ending Clock Change Aerial view of downtown Bozeman, Montana at dusk. Lawmakers in landlocked states out West, like Sens. Steve Daines, R-Mont., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warn that it would cause kids in their states to go to school in the dark. "I can see where Florida likes it for tee times at certain times of the year, but it doesn’t work so well for moms and dads putting kids on buses when the sunrise in Western Montana wouldn’t be till 9:30 in the morning. It’s not going to work for us," Daines told CNN in July. Click Here To Download The Fox News App The most vital currency in the Senate is floor time. And lawmakers won’t have much floor time to spare when they return after the midterm elections in November. Though it’s popular, more pressing issues like the National Defense Authorization Act, supplemental funding for the war and a looming government funding battle will likely take precedence. And Republican leaders acknowledge that it’s not as easy as a simple yes-or-no vote for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. "Depends where you're living in the country and the impact — what it would be, in your own home state," Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said in July. "So it's not as simple as what one state might like." item.title: Jim Bakker, televangelist who built a massive empire before scandal, dies at 86
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jim Bakker, who built a huge TV following and evangelical empire with his first wife, Tammy Faye, which later collapsed in a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86. Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. The cause of death was not provided. “He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” she said. The pair lived near Branson, an entertainment destination in Missouri, where they had filmed their TV show “The Jim Bakker Show” since its launch in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020. But it was the “The PTL Club,” which at its peak in the mid-1980s drew 13 million nightly TV viewers, that made Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 90s by late-night comedians and parodied on “Saturday Night Live.” The couple also built Heritage USA, a Christian theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina, and a movie about their lives, “The Eyes of Tammy Faye,” was released in September 2021. Bakker starts out as a traveling preacher Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry. He preached and she sang and played the accordion in churches and tent revivals across the country. They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children’s show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, Bakker was hosting “The 700 Club,” a Christian talk show. Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. “The PTL Club” — PTL stands for “Praise the Lord” — became its signature show. In its heyday in the 1980s, “The PTL Club” attracted millions of viewers and brought in millions of dollars annually. The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina. They were often parodied by TV comedians, mocked for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s abundant makeup. Sex scandal and financial crimes damage his empire Their standing began to crumble in March 1987, when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Hahn alleged that Bakker sexually assaulted her; Bakker maintained that the encounter was consensual. Bakker was forced to resign from his empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell. Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often seen with mascara-stained tears running down her face. Bakker was indicted in 1988 for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted the following year and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison. The sentence was later reduced to eight years. At a news conference after he was found guilty, Tammy Faye sang the hymn, “On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand.” Their marriage fell apart and Tammy Faye divorced the still-incarcerated Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison. Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007. Bakker was released on parole in 1994 and married Lori in 1998. They launched “The Jim Bakker Show” on the PTL Satellite Network five years later. In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic. The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March 2020. Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and Lori Bakker adopted five children in 2002. ___ Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary. item.title: Republicans pour $700 million into midterms as red states turn competitive
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump arrives to speak at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, on Sunday. (Mark Schiefelbein / AP) Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts. Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer. By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month. The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. That’s led by a massive, late investment in the Senate race in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico is threatening a longtime Republican seat and the GOP has poured in almost $150 million in new ad dollars to back up its nominee, Ken Paxton. The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP. Democrats still have a number of advantages in their corner, including President Donald Trump and his party’s eroding standing among voters, Democrats’ own well-funded candidates, and help from outside groups. Candidates can take advantage of a rule that allows them to buy television ads at cheaper rates than outside groups, too. But the color of the outside money flood shows how Republicans, increasingly on defense in both the House and the Senate, are able to lean on their financial advantage in hope of defying political gravity, as party bastions like Texas and even Kansas look more competitive than usual. On Tuesday morning, South Carolina — where a Democrat has not won a Senate race since 1998 — became the latest state to see a new infusion of Republican money, with the super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans planning to spend $5 million there, according to a source familiar with the spending. Axios first reported the spending in the state. “With the environment not on our side and an incumbent presidency, the three things we have going for us are good candidates, a good map and a lot more money than they do,” said a Republican strategist involved in Senate races. Everything about the late flood of ad spending is bigger in Texas, where a new group called Texas PAC has booked more than $115 million over the last month alone aimed at boosting Paxton, the state attorney general. Democrats haven’t won a statewide election in Texas in more than 30 years. But because Republicans are spending largely through outside groups, they have to pay a premium on the rates for each ad, while Talarico’s flush campaign is able to capitalize on those lower candidate ad rates. That means the spending disparity is greater than the actual number of ad airings or their reach. Senate races in Ohio and Michigan also drew more than $75 million in new ad dollars in September, mostly from Republican-aligned groups. They include a super PAC funded by cryptocurrency interests, Trump’s aligned super PACs and other groups aligned with the national party or Senate Republican leadership. Again, both states have Democratic candidates — former Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio and former county health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — who have been spending significant money on their advertising campaigns. No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have made more than $150 million in new ad bookings since the start of September across dozens of races. While the groups haven’t confirmed where they’ve gotten their war chest from, The New York Times recently confirmed that MAGA Inc., Trump’s main super PAC, is primarily funding the effort with the hundreds of millions of dollars it has banked over the last few years. Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, chair of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, touted the party’s spending advantage as key to helping Republicans hold on to their majority and credited Trump’s deep-pocketed political operation with ensuring the flood of cash continues. Scott told reporters that he met last week with Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and that the message from Wiles was “money will not be our problem.” “That’s exciting news to me,” Scott said, adding later, “Knowing that they are going to invest completely in these races is incredibly helpful, because cash is king.” “We finally find ourselves at a cash advantage because of MAGA Inc. It’s a powerful tool that is providing us with the firepower necessary to really share our message,” he said. Democrats take some solace in where the new spending is going. The vast majority is plowing into states and seats Trump carried in 2024, including congressional districts Trump would have won by double digits that year, like North Carolina’s 1st District, Texas’ 35th District and Alaska’s at-large congressional district. The money is also going to races in which Republicans felt comfortable until recently, like the Senate race in Kansas, where the top Senate Republican super PAC just reallocated millions initially meant to be spent in North Carolina. “The money is not because there is this swell of Republican momentum; the money is because of a swell of Republican panic,” said Lauren French, the communications director at Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership. “Voters don’t like anything they are selling — that includes the message, the candidates and the president.” Meredith Kelly, a longtime Democratic strategist who works on House and Senate races, said, “When you are defending in such deep-red territory, the technical term for that is: ‘You’re f---ed.’” “Republicans, if they have one advantage, it’s that they have more money, and they are putting that money to the test right now post-Labor Day,” Kelly added. “However, the big question is: Is that money enough to counteract the fact that Donald Trump’s coalition is falling apart?” Still, Democrats are uncomfortable watching their party get outspent to such a degree. “It’s a huge problem, and it will be an ongoing problem, and you see all the lists of high-value donors for both parties and we get swamped every time,” Kelly said. “It creates such an initial advantage for the Republicans that we have to close the gap on in a variety of ways — candidate money, better message, better candidates. We are setting ourselves up for an uphill battle every single time because of the Republican donor strength in terms of the billionaire class.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/republicans-fight-red-state-midterm-chaos-hundreds-millions-late-money-rcna601675

item.title: Multiple countries consider restrictions on smart glasses amid privacy concerns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Oct 6 (Reuters) - Governments, courts and companies are considering restrictions and examining existing rules on smart glasses amid worries that the technology, ‌brought to mainstream by Meta's Ray-Bans, could be used to photograph, film or ‌audio-record confidential materials or people without their knowledge. Here is a summary of what countries and regions ​are doing to protect people's privacy, in alphabetical order. AUSTRALIA The federal government said in September it was considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces due to privacy and security concerns. Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher asked the country's Public ‌Service Commission for advice on ⁠whether their use should be prohibited and what exemptions might be required. BRITAIN Courts in England and Wales have prohibited the use ⁠of Meta smart glasses because of restrictions on taking images and videos in courts. British cinema operators are also introducing policies to prohibit or restrict camera-enabled smart glasses, the ​UK ​Cinema Association said in August. EUROPEAN UNION Smart glasses ​have attracted scrutiny from European privacy ‌regulators and some lawmakers, and the European Data Protection Board has commissioned a report into their "social acceptability". Member of the European Parliament Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová also urged the European Commission, which has not proposed legislation specifically targeting smart glasses, to consider possible action. NORWAY The government said it planned to propose a temporary ban on the ‌use of AI glasses in places where the ​public regularly gather, such as parks, beaches, museums, ​shopping centres and public events. Norway's ​capital Oslo banned smart glasses in schools in August. UNITED STATES New ‌York's Unified Court System banned smart glasses ​from all its ​court facilities from July 20. The rule covers prescription and non-prescription eyewear or headwear containing cameras, microphones, computers or other technology capable of recording ​video or audio. Visitors ‌carrying them must hand them over to court personnel for safekeeping ​before entering. item.title: Sen. Tillis calls deciding vote for Hegseth the 'biggest regret' of his career
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth’s turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations. “I know for a fact that there are others like me,” Tillis writes, “Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far.” He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have “expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president’s actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they’d have nothing but nice things to say.” Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a “breaking point” with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically. Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, “my beef is not with him, but the idiots he’s got working for him.” He calls the president “an amazing political talent.” At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to “wake up” and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, “comes back to bite the majority party in the ass.” Tillis also predicts a “bloodbath” for Republicans in November’s midterm elections . “All along, we’ve had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down,” he writes. Regrets his votes for Hegseth and Kennedy The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump’s tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to “intentionally sow disorder” and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets “Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way.” Tillis pushed Hegseth’s confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn’t corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie. On his vote for Kennedy , Tillis writes that “I guess it’s easy to say now, but I’m the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy’s tenure has caused the country as a result.” On both votes, he says he didn’t want to be the deciding factor. “I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward,” he writes. If you oppose Trump on everything, “you lose all influence,” Tillis says. “If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape.” He strongly criticizes several of Trump’s other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Tillis describes his 'breaking point' over the tax bill Tillis’s surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn’t be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his “ Big Beautiful Bill ” of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn’t support the bill’s cuts to Medicaid . Tillis says he thought to himself, “I’m done.” “Everyone reaches a breaking point,” he writes. He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied “I am! DJT.” In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a “QUITTER!” on social media, among other insults. Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response. “I care if you fail and right now we are failing,” Tillis wrote to Trump. item.title: U.K. police make 7th arrest over suspected plot targeting U.S. air base
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LONDON (AP) — British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offense over a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that authorities have linked to Iran . The arrest is the seventh in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford , located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during this year's war. Five British men in their 20s were detained near the perimeter of the base in the early hours of Sept. 27, and a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London on Thursday. All six have been released on bail under investigation. Counter Terrorism Policing said a British national was detained Tuesday in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives “continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry” and “remain committed to investigating all possible angles.” Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area late at night. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the United Kingdom saw “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was. Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target . The United States moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it's unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he didn’t want to tempt “the enemy” by having the bombers there. “We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he said in Washington. He said that the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” but he didn’t offer details. British officials have declined to comment on reports that the bombers were moved because of fears of a drone attack on the base. The prime minister's spokesman, Tom Wells, said Monday he was "not going to comment on foreign nations’ military operations.” But he insisted that RAF Fairford is safe. The mysterious incident near the base came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025. U.K. officials also say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue. item.title: Russia says no plague cases detected among contacts of deceased lab worker
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
SHELEKHOV, Russia, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died last week, ‌and locals said their lives had barely been disrupted. Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of ‌an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump. Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious ​diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 days and that extensive testing had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work. "A comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately organised and implemented in full in accordance with public health legislation," the watchdog said. "This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been ‌in contact with the patient and arranging ⁠for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests." It said the results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing ⁠other infectious diseases had been detected. "None of the contacts showed any changes in their state of health associated with infectious disease," it added. Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said what she called a "dangerous diagnosis" had not been ​confirmed. She ​added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as a precaution had ​already been released. Local media said around 200 people ‌had previously been quarantined. TRUMP'S OFFER OF HELP Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it. "It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters. Trump on Monday described the situation as a "big problem for Russia". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information. The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no cases of plague in ‌the city of Irkutsk. Reuters could not immediately establish if this meant ​they could rule out plague in the lab worker's case. In the town of ​Shelekhov, where the lab worker is reported to have died ​in hospital, locals said their lives had barely been disrupted although they said some people in shops ‌had initially worn surgical face masks as a precaution. A ​resident who gave her name only ​as Anna said the situation was calm and that people had been prepared for restrictions to be introduced, but that life had gone on pretty much as usual. "Everyone had face masks at home and wore them for no more than ​24 hours," she told Reuters. Denis, another resident, ‌said news of the lab worker's death had been widely discussed in the town and that the local hospital ​had temporarily stopped doing diagnostic tests but had since resumed normal business. (Reporting by Vladimir Soldatkin and Anastasia Lyrchikova; ​Writing by Mark Trevelyan and Andrew Osborn, Editing by Timothy Heritage) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/russia-says-no-plague-cases-103151967.html

item.title: Chicago woman shot 5 times by Border Patrol agent files federal lawsuit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CHICAGO ( WGN ) — A Chicago woman who was shot five times by a Border Patrol agent during Operation Midway Blitz filed a lawsuit against the federal government Monday, calling for more action against the agent who shot her. Marimar Martinez said the encounter with Border Patrol agents happened in Oct. 2025. She was allegedly heading to church to drop off clothing donations when she noticed immigration officers on her street. “For the next 15 to 20 minutes, I followed these Border Patrol agents through my neighborhood, honking my horn, shouting out ‘La Migra,’” Martinez said while testifying on Capitol Hill in Feb. Martinez said the driver of the Border Patrol vehicle she was following made eye contact with her before swerving into and hitting her truck. “I drove forward and went around the Border Patrol agent who jumped out of his car and pointed his gun at me. I moved to the far-left lane, striking the curb on the far-left side of Kedzie (Avenue). The next thing I knew, I felt a burning sensation in my arms and legs,” Martinez said. “As I continued trying to drive past the Border Patrol agents, I could hear my back passenger window shatter, and I felt bullets continue to pierce my body.” Chicago woman recounts violent encounter with Border Patrol before Congress The Department of Homeland Security called her a domestic terrorist and charged her with using her vehicle to assault federal agents. However, the Department of Justice later dropped all charges against her. While addressing the civil lawsuit outside a downtown Chicago law office Monday, attorneys representing Martinez said they are seeking more transparency and accountability. “We are here today, exactly one year and one day after the shooting of Marimar by agent Charles Exum. As you all know, there has been absolutely zero progress from the Department of Justice as far as accountability goes,” attorney Chris Parente said. “There’s been no investigation. There’s been no charges.” Judge delays decision on releasing sealed Border Patrol shooting bodycam footage The lawsuit alleges that Border Patrol’s account of the shooting contradicts what Martinez says actually happened. The Department of Homeland Security said that during the immigration crackdown altercation, Martinez tried to ram agents with her vehicle. Martinez maintains that she was driving away from them when one of the agents fired into her vehicle. “What we’ve done here as a defense team is that we essentially became our own Department of Justice. We have hired our own experts, we have done our own investigation,” Parente said. DHS Sec. Noem’s lack of knowledge on Chicago shootings raises eyebrows Martinez’s attorneys presented new video and photo evidence from the incident, saying it shows the agent was not in harm’s way when he started shooting. Martinez said she and her family saw the material for the first time Sunday. “It brought a lot of clarity for them. They got a lot of answers on what happened on Oct. 4,” Martinez said. Read more coverage from WGN on Operation Midway Blitz Martinez said she’s thankful to be alive to share her story and wants to fight for others affected by Operation Midway Blitz. “I want to spread awareness because what’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t sit here and normalize what’s happening,” Martinez said. Read more: Latest Chicago news and headlines Martinez and her attorneys have been planning to sue for months.
